newsitem.title: USA: SEC Chairman sees "profound" rules changes.
newsitem.headline: SEC Chairman sees "profound" rules changes.

text.p: The next few years are likely to bring broad changes in the rules governing U.S. financial markets, the securities industry's top regulator said on Thursday.

Speaking to indsutry executives at the Securities Industry Association annual meeting here, Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Arthur Levitt said he expected "a profound rethinking of the way financial markets are regulated in the next few years."

Calling regulatory change "inevitable" Levitt said he would be disappointed if, for example, the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) did not modify its circuit breaker rules. He also said the new Congress would likely produce a bill reforming the Glass Steagall Act.
"As we enter the period of the new Congress there will be a lot of ideas," Levitt said. He warned, however, that changing the act would require caution.
"The cultures of banking and investment banking are so different the lines between have been carefully drawn and should be preserved," he said.
Several possible rules changes Levitt mentioned related directly to derivatives.

One under consideration would establish an entirely new class of broker-dealers specifically to facilitate derivatives transactions, while another would alter so-called net capital rules governing investment banks.
"The capital rules were put in place in a time of different needs," said Levitt.

Among the perceived flaws in existing law he noted were capital requirements governing derivatives positions. Under current rules, firms that engage in two completely off-setting transactions must allocate a capital reserve for each transaction even though the firm bears essentially no net capital risk.
A possible new rule would end that requirement, offering a somewhat freer hand to U.S. firms who, he said, have complained current law is pushing business to outfits outside the U.S.

While Levitt focused on simplifying rules in some areas he said the SEC would likely intensify its efforts as in the scruntiny of "soft dollar" arrangements between firms and the use of aggressive compensation programs to lure brokers away from competitors.
The programs have resulted in high turnover rates at brokerages which Levitt said was one of the obstacles to building trust in the industry.
Levitt also referred to the SEC's actions in the Nasdaq market case where dealers were caught on tape arranging to keep bid and offer spreads artificially high.
However, he offered few details about what might come next, saying "the ball is now in the NASD's court" as far as implementing reforms to eliminate the chance of market abuse occurring again.
"Investors and issuers alike are watching carefully to see if reform is structural or superficial," he said.
